title: Karna's plate of gold
hookLine: Karna is served gold in heaven because he never fed his ancestors, and Mimamsa names what carries an offering on: apurva
tomorrow: a scholar falls from a tower with one word on his lips. which word did he regret?

cards: Karna, the warrior well-known for never refusing anyone who asked him for anything, dies in battle and rises to heaven. He's hungry, and they bring him food. It's gold.
Plates of gold and jewels, and nothing he can eat. He asks why. The answer comes back: on earth you gave gold to everyone, but you never once offered food to your ancestors.
Karna had never even known who his ancestors were. So he's allowed back to earth for fifteen days, to offer them food and water.
Many families tell this story to explain Pitru Paksha, the fortnight each year for honoring the ancestors.

teach.b: The story isn't in the Mahabharata itself; it's a popular telling. But it carries a question Mimamsa asked with great care. The Veda says, in effect, the one who desires heaven should perform this offering.
Fine. The offering is done. The fire burns down and everyone goes home.
But the result it was for comes much later, maybe after this life. How can something that no longer exists bring anything about? Shabara, in his commentary on Jaimini, gives the answer.
It produces something unseen, which stays and carries the act forward until its fruit arrives. Its name is apurva: the new thing, something that wasn't there before the act and is there after.
You can't film it or prove it by argument. It's known, Mimamsa says, because the Veda asks for the act and promises its fruit.

That fits yesterday: dharma couldn't be seen, and apurva is how its good travels through time. Other schools speak of the lasting effect of action in their own ways, and the word karma covers much of that ground.
And this shape, an act that ends while what it set moving travels on, is the shape a family trusts at a shraddha. The rice balls are set out. The water is poured.
The priest goes home. And Hindus hold that the offering reaches the ones it was made for. Karna came back from heaven to make sure his did.

how: Hindus offer food and water to the ancestors at shraddha and during Pitru Paksha; Mimamsa teachers, following Shabara, explain that a rite properly done produces apurva, an unseen potency that lasts after the act and brings its result in time.

o: a school where a rite's power ends with the chant
a school where an act leaves an unseen force, apurva
a school where the fruit must come before the fire dies

games.q: gold, rice and apurva — tap the pairs.
p: served gold, not food, in heaven
the unseen new thing that carries an act

s: in Mimamsa, a finished ritual simply vanishes
Shabara says it produces apurva, which stays until its fruit comes.
the story of Karna's gold is told in the Mahabharata itself
it's a popular telling, often shared at Pitru Paksha.
apurva is how Mimamsa explains a result that comes long after the act
it bridges the gap between a finished act and its later fruit.

games.q: the shraddha is done and the priest has gone home. in Mimamsa's way of thinking, is the rite over and gone?
o: yes: once the fire is out, nothing remains
no: the act set something unseen moving, apurva, that carries it on
only the priest's memory of it remains
games.why: apurva. in Shabara's account, the act leaves something unseen that carries it forward until the fruit arrives.

practice: In the spirit of tarpana, the water offering to the ancestors: hold a little water in your cupped right hand, name a grandparent or someone you've lost, and let the water pour out, three times.
If you pray, offer it to them with a short prayer. If you don't, simply say their name and thank you, and let the act be complete as an act.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the new or unprecedented; in Mimamsa, the unseen potency a rite produces.

carryVoice: Your line: apurva, the offering travels on. The rite ends; what it set moving doesn't. That's today, done.
